claims.text: Conventional tempered martensitic low-alloy or carbon steel can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition within a narrow temperature window.
Temper embrittlement causes the narrow-temperature loss of ductility in this steel.
The transition is caused by grain-boundary segregation of impurity elements.
Tempered martensitic steel is a suitable model system for studying sharp loss and recovery of ductility with temperature.
Conventional heat treatment produces tempered martensite with associated impurity segregation at grain boundaries.
The steel is ductile at temperatures below the temper-embrittlement window.
Brittleness peaks within the temper-embrittlement temperature range.
Ductility recovers at temperatures above the temper-embrittlement window.
Phosphorus, tin, or other embrittling impurity atoms segregate to grain boundaries during tempering.
The segregated impurity atoms precipitate during tempering.
At intermediate temperatures, impurity segregation weakens intergranular cohesion.
Weakening of intergranular cohesion produces a sharp decrease in ductility.
At lower temperatures, diffusion is too sluggish for significant impurity segregation.
At higher temperatures, impurities redistribute or grain boundaries heal, allowing ductility to recover.
The transition requires controlled impurity levels and may disappear when impurity content is too high or too low.
The transition may not occur in high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys employing advanced alloying strategies.
The embrittlement-window temperature and magnitude of the ductility loss vary with impurity content, alloy composition, and thermal treatment.

contradictions.description: The initial state is said to already contain impurity segregation produced by prior heat treatment, whereas the mechanism attributes the absence of low-temperature embrittlement to segregation being insignificant because diffusion is sluggish. Pre-existing segregation would not necessarily disappear merely because the subsequent testing temperature is low.

The structural mediator describes segregated impurity atoms as precipitating, while the mechanism treats them as solute atoms that segregate and later redistribute. Segregation and precipitation are distinct states, and the hypothesis does not reconcile them.
